reconcile.connective: Commentators read the shifting order and final item in each list as an inconsequential rearrangement rather than a disagreement, noting Scripture itself reorders the very same commandments elsewhere.

discrepancy.connective: Steve Wells, in the Skeptic's Annotated Bible, presses the sharper problem behind the ordering: Luke's list stops at five items altogether, so there is no 'sixth' commandment there to compare against Matthew's and Mark's competing candidates.

skeptic.name: Steve Wells
skeptic.work: The Skeptic's Annotated Bible, "What was Jesus's sixth commandment?" (skepticsannotatedbible.com/contra/sixth.html)
skeptic.attribution: Steve Wells, The Skeptic's Annotated Bible (online; contra/sixth.html)

excerpts.excerpt_text: This, as it is the first commandment with promise, so the first of the second table, and yet is here mentioned last; which inversion of order is of no consequence: so the "seventh" command is put before the "sixth", and the "fifth" omitted, in Rom 13:9 …
excerpts.on_tension_rationale: Directly answers the 'which is sixth' framing: Gill argues the placement of 'honour thy father and mother' last in Matthew's list is an inconsequential inversion of order, citing Paul's own reordering of the commandments in Romans 13:9 as precedent that recital order carries no doctrinal weight.

pd_work.resource: John Gill, Exposition of the Entire Bible (1746-63), on Matthew 19:19 and Mark 10:18
pd_work.author: John Gill
pd_work.note: Gill treats the commandment-order variation directly at both Matthew 19:19 and Mark 10:18, invoking the rabbinic maxim that there is 'neither first nor last in the law' and citing Paul's own reordering in Romans 13:9. (Haley's Alleged Discrepancies does not appear to treat this specific passage — checked against the full text for 'defraud,' 'sixth commandment,' and the relevant roman-numeral verse citations with no hits — so per spec the row-surfaced harmonizing commentator keyed to the passage is used instead.)
